utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: The Djakovica region, while I was there, was extremely important to the terrorists because it was the main communication line and along the road which enabled the unhindered passage and control of the territory on their part, from their side. And anybody in control of that road and the communication lines was able to control the entire territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How far were you aware of the situation in Djakovica during the war and the surrounding parts?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Well, in the town of Djakovica itself, there were not that many terrorist forces. However, in the surrounding places, such as Smonica, Ponosevac, Nec, Kislavane [phoen], Sisman Baks, Popovac, those were their strongholds. Smonica was one of their strongest strongholds, in actual fact, at least in the area of responsibility covered by our unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 63(h), it says here that up until March, by March 1999, by March, the population of the town of Djakovica had increased significantly due to the large number of internally displaced persons who fled their villages to escape deliberate shelling by forces of the FRY and Serbia during 1998 and to escape the armed conflict between these forces and members of the KLA. Were you personally present in Djakovica? Were you there yourself during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Yes, I was, Mr. Milosevic. I was in Djakovica with my unit at the time, or rather, we were outside Djakovica proper. However, what is stated, alleged there, it is true that the population was leaving those places, but there was none of this shelling, and I don't understand the term "shelling." I don't know what it means. They weren't fleeing from pressure from us, but from pressure on the terrorists that would use them to build fortification lines and do strenuous physical labour and ask them to give money contributions and contributions in food. So the inhabitants, due to all these pressures and threats from the terrorists, pulled out of these places, not wishing to work for them. And anybody who was able to reach Djakovica went, because in Smonica we didn't come across a single inhabitant. At Ramoc we did find the inhabitants and the inhabitants told me about this themselves. As I was in the village of Ramoc for a time, the inhabitants themselves, in talking to me, told me that the terrorists constantly issued threats and made them do strenuous physical work, sent them to Albania to fetch weapons, and if they didn't wish to go, they would take their sons and force them bring in weapons for them. Or rather, they would pay a certain amount of money -- they had to pay a certain amount of money if they didn't want to agree to the conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So those people who didn't want to have work of that kind to do had to pay, and you're thinking about the inhabitants, are you?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Yes, the inhabitants of those surrounding parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In that same paragraph, 63(h), it says that the continual movement of these internally displaced persons increased after the 24th of March, 1999, when, following violent expulsions in the town of Djakovica, many internally displaced persons returned from the town of Djakovica to the outlying villages only to be expelled from these villages again by forces of the FRY and Serbia. Do you know of any forceful expulsions?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: No, I don't, because I passed through the town sometime around 2.00, with all my equipment, when I went to take up my assignment. I didn't notice any movement on the part of the population, nor did I notice anybody being expulsed, as it is alleged there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then they fled to the village and it says that our forces once again expelled them from those villages. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it's quite natural that people will leave there places to take safety because the NATO air strikes started at that time in the town of Djakovica. And on the evening -- in the evening, at 8.00, there were NATO air strikes against our barracks in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is a well-known fact. I won't dwell on that. Several witnesses have already told us about that. But let me just ask you this: In paragraph 63 again, (ii), it says in the early hours of the 27th of April, 1999, the forces of FRY and Serbia launched a large-scale offensive in the valley of Carragojs, Erenik, Trava in the Djakovica municipality, aimed at expelling the population from that area. Do you know anything about that? Were you in the region? Do you know what was happening on the 27th of April, 1999, in the valleys of Carragojs, Erenik and Trava?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, my units were securing the frontier at Maja Kraljica, Cafe Rance, in depth to Guska. So in the early hours of the morning of the 27th of April, a group of terrorists, eight to ten of them, tried to break through across the area of -- the line of defence of my unit towards the state border and to flee to Albania. On that occasion, two members of my own unit were wounded. The group was routed and it returned to the region it had come from. And as to any action in the area, I know nothing of that because my unit did not take part in any combat action.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite clear. So when that action started, the group tried to break through your area of defence and had to go back; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Yes. The group was broken up and it had to go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about this concentration of terrorist forces in the Carragojs, Erenik and Trava valleys?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: I know nothing about that. I didn't go to the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. In paragraph 105 of the indictment, it says that in addition to the forceful expulsion -- in addition to the forced expulsion of Kosovo Albanians, forces of the FRY and Serbia also engaged in a number of killings of Kosovo Albanians since the 24th of March, 1999, at numerous locations, including Bela Crkva, Mala Krusa, Djakovica. Here, Velika Krusa, Djakovica -- I don't want to read all the names listed here. I'm just going to read out the names where you yourself were, that is to say, Bela Crkva, Mala Krusa, Velika Krusa, and Djakovica. Now, please, was our army taking part in, as it says here, a number of killings of Kosovo Albanians at that time?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: I am not aware of any of that, Mr. Milosevic. First of all, my unit never received such an assignment and I would never carry out an assignment of that kind, because it goes against the grain of all regulations and rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, let me ask you a question from another angle. Did the army use force or threats in any way to force Kosovo Albanians to move out?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In view of your own position in the army, did you ever hear of any such intention or plan, or any activity which could be linked up with any forcible expulsion of Kosovo Albanians?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: I never heard about that, nor did I ever see anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned, on several occasions during your testimony, the MUP. Now, what was the relationship between you and the police, on the ground, in the area you were in, in the area you engaged in your activities?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, with the MUP, or with the units I cooperated with, we had very good cooperation. We had -- engaged in joint anti-terrorist operations and exchanged information and intelligence about the situation on the ground in that area. I had no command responsibility vis-a-vis them, but we worked on the same assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about your superiors? Did they, like you, receive daily information coming in from the field about what was going on?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: It was my duty as commander, Mr. Milosevic, company commander, or rather, commander of that unit, was that I should, at all times, report back to the unit commander about the situation in the unit and on the ground, in the aim of providing a proper picture of what was going on so that steps and measures could be taken towards the realisation of future tasks and assignments. We used couriers, we used communication lines or personal contacts with my superiors, and they would be informed of what was going on in my area of responsibility on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So there were no exceptions. You didn't give timely, comprehensive information on a daily basis about the situation in your area [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: No, there were no exceptions to that. That was an ongoing task and assignment of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Among the charges in the indictment, there is frequent mention -- for example, in paragraph 53, but that's not the only paragraph, so I'm not going to quote all the paragraphs. But anyway, there's constant mention of deliberate and widespread -- so deliberate and widespread campaign of terror and violence directed at Kosovo Albanian civilians living in Kosovo in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, which was imposed through the forces of the FRY and Serbia, who took on operations aimed against the Kosovo Albanian population, with the aim of expelling a large portion of the population from Kosovo and to ensure Serb control over the province. Now, were you aware of or knew about any kind of activity, let alone operation, because the word here used, I believe, was "operations," any activities directed against Kosovo Albanians or Albanians in Kosovo and Metohija except the operation against terrorists? So I'm asking you now about the general Albanian Kosovo population.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I had no knowledge, nor was I aware of any activities or intention on the basis of units to carry out such assignments. Everything that we did was geared towards an anti-terrorist struggle and safeguarding the border from a land aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 55, it also says that the forces of the FRY and Serbia, in a deliberate and widespread or systematic manner, forcibly expelled and internally displaced hundreds of thousands of Kosovo Albanians from their homes across the entire province of Kosovo, and that they created an atmosphere of fear and oppression through the use of force, threats of force, and acts of violence. Now, your unit was there, your unit was carrying out assignments in the area. Did your unit, at any point in time during the war, or before the war, for that matter, create an atmosphere of fear, instilled fear in the population, even if you didn't shoot? Did you try to intimidate the population to instil fear in them to force them to move out, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: No, Mr. Milosevic. There was nothing of that kind. We even provided security in those areas, such as Ramoc and the places around Smonica from onslaughts by the terrorists and mistreatment of the population by the terrorists. So we did not engage in any of the activities alleged here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 56, it says throughout Kosovo, forces of the FRY and Serbia engaged in destruction of property owned by Kosovo Albanian civilians. This was accomplished by the widespread shelling of towns and villages, the burning and destruction of property, including homes, farms, businesses, cultural monuments, et cetera, et cetera. You, as an officer of the army of Yugoslavia in your particular unit, did you at any point in time shell towns and villages, burn and destroy property belonging to the Albanians in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, action in towns was action by NATO aeroplanes. We did not engage in any action except anti-terrorist combat and firing at their own firing points. So even when we engaged in anti-terrorist combat, we strictly targeted the terrorist strongholds and firing points. And as to the shelling and everything else, that was done by NATO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I've had occasion previously to tell you that this kind of evidence is practically meaningless. You have led useful evidence from this witness in relation to matters in which he was involved. Getting his general view on paragraph 46 [sic], which concerns matters in which he wasn't involved, is not helpful in any way to your case. And if the rest of your examination-in-chief relates to this kind of evidence, then I would strongly advise that you stop and let Mr. Nice begin his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll stop very soon. But the indictment presents things in general terms, that the forces of the army did all these things that I quoted, so it is useful, when we have a witness who is a member of these forces and who commanded a unit, to find out whether he was engaged in any such thing. He is certainly not an exception. I cannot bring everybody in, all the commanders and all the squad leaders from Kosovo to testify here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, you were at the border?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How much time did you spend at the border during the course of the war?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: According to the plan, after anti-terrorist fighting, we took up the state border, and from the 5th of April, 1999, until the units withdrew from Kosovo and Metohija, we were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now let me not refer to all these paragraphs again that have to do with expulsions of Albanians. But at this border that you were at, did you manage to find out whether any forces of the Yugoslav army escorted Albanians to the border, thus trying to exercise control over their movement and so on and so forth? You were there. You were the one who was at the border. You're watching civilians who are fleeing. Was the army escorting them, keeping them under their control? Did they insist that they should cross the border or was there any such thing taking place?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: In the area where my unit was, there were no columns, there were no forcible expulsions of civilians. This is a hilly, mountainous area. There are no paths there. And I did not see any such thing, either on the left or on the right, where my neighbours were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of the destruction of documents of Albanians?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As an officer, did you ever receive any orders to deport Albanians from Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: No, I never received such orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of any kind of plan of ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have information all the time about what was going on on the terrain where you were?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: I had information all the time, from my superior command and also by way of personal contact with my left- and right-hand neighbours, because every day we talked about the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel Sel.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Colonel Sel, what, if any, documents have you brought with you that were prepared at the time of these events?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I, as company commander, do not have any written documents. All reports, all documents that I had, I sent to my superior command and they kept the war diary, and I did not do that kind of thing in my unit. So all this information was transmitted orally to the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you saying that you kept, as a company commander, no written record of anything that you did?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: I made written notes. I wrote notes and I sent them to the superior command. These are the regular daily reports while we were in that area. However, when combat activity was taking place, then we reported orally. And then, when, in accordance with the plan, we took our positions at the state border, then written reports were sent in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the written reports, the daily combat reports, they should all still exist?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: No. My reports do not exist. All these reports from subordinate units are entered into the daily operative report of the battalion command, because it brings all of that together, introduces some elements in the war diary, or rather, sends it to the superior command in its own report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what, they then destroy your documents, do they?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So the best contemporaneous record and the only existing contemporaneous record in written form of what you did is to be found where? Whose diary, and where?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: All these reports, Mr. Nice, characteristic reports pertaining to the area of responsibility of my unit, can be found in the war diary of the command of the battalion of my unit, of Colonel Vlatko Vukovic, and in the daily reports sent to his superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Vukovic's materials include an ingoing and -- incoming and outgoing log of reports, including company reports. Did you, so far as you can recall, contribute to that body of written material?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You made some statements - we've seen them, five in number - to the expert committee of the VJ Commission on Cooperation. When you made those statements, did you refer to any contemporaneous material?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I did not refer to any such thing. These statements were written on the basis of my memory, on the basis of what I experienced. I did not have any contact with the war diary or the reports that were sent to the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So everything in each of those five statements just comes from memory, does it?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Not from a piece of paper and not from any other individual; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't talk to anybody when I wrote those statements. Because everybody wrote their statements on their own, so I do not know what others wrote.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Why were they written in five different statements as opposed to one single one? What was the subject for each statement? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: I think that they sought the daily engagement of the units in order to see what the daily activities in the area were, and that is why individual statements were written for each and every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If that was the instruction, who gave you the instruction as to how to prepare these statements?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: No one gave me instructions as to how I should write those statements. I wrote the statements on the basis of my memory, for each and every day, from the 25th through the 28th of March, to write about what my unit did in terms of anti-terrorist combat during those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who told you to prepare a statement for the 25th, prepare a statement for the 26th? Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: On the basis of the order of the superior command. I received orders from the superior command at the request of the expert team; my superior commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: My superior commander was Colonel Delic. However, at that time, Colonel Delic, or rather, General Delic, was reassigned to the General Staff. So I didn't have contact with him but, rather, with my superior officer who came in then, Colonel Djurovic. Or, rather, at that time he was not commander. It was Colonel Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: These maps we've been looking at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the answer to the question? The question was: Who asked you to prepare the reports?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My superior command did, at the request of the expert team. So a request arrived at my superior command that officers who took part in combat activities in that area should write reports, or rather, statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In our own way, we've been trying to find, His Honour and I, the name of the commander. Any reason why you shouldn't give it to us? From Delic and via who?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: No, Mr. Nice, it didn't come from General Delic. My superior commander asked me -- told me that, at the request of the expert team, all officers who took part in combat activities in the area should make statements for each and every individual day and for the activities that they were involved in on each one of these days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've taken a long time to find out that I can't get the name of the officer, but I'll just move on, I think, and spend my limited time in some other way. You made an observation about there being no mosque in Celine.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You're saying there was simply no mosque and never was a mosque in Celine; is that it?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: No, there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... pictures, please. They come from Exhibit 88, tab -- it's not a tab, it's just part of Exhibit 88. Thank you. This is an expert who's given evidence, and he shows a picture here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I'm not sure whether the witness understood exactly what you were asking about the -- you were trying to find out who his superior commander was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I was asking for his name, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think he mentioned one name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the name of your superior commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, sir, Mr. Robinson, my commander was Stojan Konjikovac, Colonel Stojan Konjikovac. That's what I said a few minutes ago. At the time when I wrote the report at the request of the expert team and on orders from my superior command, it was Stojan Konjikovac. It's not that I was trying to hide it or any such thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I thought so, yes. Please go.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The photograph here, according to the witness who has given evidence before this Court, is a photograph of the damaged mosque, burnt down and in ruins, bulldozed by the Serbs, according to the Islamic community. And the next photograph shows it enlarged. Sorry, this is the larger photograph, and it shows the round formation of a minaret. Do you say there was simply no mosque in Celine, looking at this photograph?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I trust my eyes more, because I walked throughout the area. I was there on foot. I therefore know more than others do. I did not have a bulldozer to destroy a mosque that never existed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, Mr. Nice says that some minaret can be seen here. Where is this minaret? I cannot see it, or perhaps I have something different on my monitor. Perhaps it's not the photograph that Mr. Nice is showing. I guess he's not referring to this chimney or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm referring to the circular formation of brickwork that we can see in the centre of the photograph, and perhaps other material to the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you make reference to a minaret?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I did. I said it's a photograph and I actually made reference to the circular or semicircular formation of the material there. The round formation of a minaret. Yes, it's the round formation of the brickwork that we can see in the centre of the picture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. What's the page number of this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This exhibit is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's K0209346, and the enlargement is KO218743.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Any explanation, for example, for this photograph at all, since it is said to come from Celine, the photograph taken in 1999?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, even if I had a tank or an anti-aircraft gun, I couldn't have done something like this. That is one point. My other point is that this looks like anything but a mosque, and it looks like the effects of an air attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So the information coming to the expert was that the site had been subsequently -- the mosque having been burnt down, it was subsequently bulldozed by Serbs. Can you help us at all with that?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I repeat once again: There were no bulldozers in that area. Others were using bulldozers to destroy Orthodox churches. I have no need to destroy places of worship. Places of worship were destroyed only if they did not respect a place of worship and started firing from it at us. And it is only then that we responded with fire. I had no intention to destroy mosques or anything down there. I repeat once again: There was no mosque in Celine. Had there been any such thing, it would have been on the topographic map. And, as Mr. Milosevic said a few moments ago, they -- he said that the reference was that it was an old mosque, and our maps date back to 1985 and that period, so it would have to be in those maps. And a hamlet of 20 houses building a mosque of its own, I really doubt it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why do you say that this looks more like the result of an air attack? It would help me if you could explain that. What is it about the destruction that makes it resemble more like the result of an air attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, on the basis of everything I saw down there - the effects of our weapons, the effects of NATO air force - our weapons opened direct fire and they could not destroy such a strongly fortified building. If there had been a mosque, it was built of sturdier material, not of straw, not of wood. And it is well known what the effects of direct shooting are and what the effects of NATO air force strikes are. This photograph looks more like --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You see, there is an issue between the parties on this matter. The Prosecution is saying that this was a result of shelling, and you are saying it looks more like the result of an air attack. Bulldozed. But I'm interested in finding out why you say this looks more like the result of an air attack, as distinct from being bulldozed, which is the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, first and foremost, I'm not sure this is a picture of Celine. I'm not familiar with this picture or anything. Whoever wants to can say that this is Celine, but I know that there was no mosque in Celine. And the only firing that took place in Celine was at firing points. So had there been a mosque there, nobody would have fired at it, nobody would have destroyed it. Secondly, even if you have a bulldozer, you have to use it to destroy a building. And what does this look like? It doesn't look like the effect of an artillery weapon or any such thing. It's a different kind of destruction. This is more like the effects of a bomb of larger calibre.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's true, isn't it, that you used your tanks in the course of this operation, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, an attack has to be distinguished between -- actually, you have to know what an attack is and what other things are. We did not attack inhabited areas. We attacked buildings where people fired at us from.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... tanks were used.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I first used tanks in Donje Retimlje, when they used anti-armour weapons against me. On the 25th of March, 1999, I was the only one who had three tanks. So on that day, tanks were not being used at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is there any written record made of such a serious operation as the use of a tank and the firing of shells from tanks?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, as for daily reports and oral communications with our commander, we always had to say how much ammunition we had spent on that day in order to possibly get new supplies. So it would not be proper for me -- it would not pay off to use a tank. It is very hard to get new ammunition when there are constant NATO air strikes and that has to be taken account of. So we used tank guns only at a minimum, when we really had to. And we only used them against firing points that we could not use other weapons to fire at with.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Artillery was also used in this overall operation, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: No, Mr. Nice. Our unit had no artillery. It had a mortar group for fire support, and this mortar group was behind me. It was 300 or 400 metres behind my unit, and it did not engage in any kind of activity at all during the course of all of these days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of the 21 tanks that Delic recorded being used, how many were in your particular company?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Three tanks were in my company, so that is to say one tank platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I may come back to these details if time allows. I want to deal with something else first. When did you join the army?

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hesitate to interrupt the testimony. Just before we move on from Celine, can I just try and assist the Court, bring to the Court's attention, that the testimony of Mr. Riedlmayer, he in fact did not visit this site, and where the bulldozing reference comes from in his report, it comes from an unnamed source and in fact the reliance is on secondary information which Mr. Riedlmayer, when he testified on the 9th of the 4th,'02, conceded himself, and he in fact described what can be seen in the picture as "either a fragment of an arch or maybe the minaret's broken. It's hard to tell."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what I was trying to find out, whether there is anything in the size and shape of the remnants, the particles, which would lead to the conclusion that this was the result of an air attack as distinct from being bulldozed or from artillery shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Hard to do on one photograph, and of course this is information coming from sources at the time and at the scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Sel, I want to turn now to your record generally. When did you join the army?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: I joined the army after I completed the military academy; on the 30th of July, 1983.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you serve in Croatia in the course of the conflict there at all?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: My place of service was always in the Republic of Serbia. However, on one occasion, following the orders of the Ministry of National Defence, I was transferred to Brekovac-Zadar to carry out a mission. That was in October --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the year.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I was mostly engaged in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please repeat the year. We didn't hear that. You said that was in October.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] October 1991. I went up there at the request of the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How long were you there?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: From October to mid-March 1992. And my primary task was to secure the civilian airport, together with my unit, which was not otherwise engaged in any fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you thereafter deployed in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Upon our return, when that group of soldiers was disbanded, I returned to my original unit in the Pirot garrison, and from there I took another unit, sometime in the beginning of March, or maybe mid-March, 1992. I went -- or rather, was transferred to the area of Tuzla, where we stayed until the 15th of May of the same year. And that unit of mine was engaged to secure transport convoys that carried supplies to units which were in positions on various axes. And again, we did not engage in fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were paid throughout by the Serbian army; correct?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: I was paid by the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, when did you first find yourself serving in the area that we are concerned with? You may have given the evidence, but it didn't appear on the transcript and it came out too fast. At least, I think so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said he was paid by the Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA. Because in March 1992, the Yugoslav army, or rather, the army of Yugoslavia, still did not exist. It was still the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army, and he was an officer of the Yugoslav People's Army. The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was proclaimed in end April 1992 and the army of Yugoslavia, under the constitution that was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you saying the witness had already given this evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said "Yugoslav People's Army."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just correcting the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the Yugoslav army is understood to be the VJ, like the army of Yugoslavia, whereas the JNA is the armed forces of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, which, at the time to which the witness is speaking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thanks, Mr. Milosevic. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's not quite clear from your evidence, Mr. Sel, when you first came to work in this area, that is, the Djakovica area. You were in Kosovo from 1997. When did you first find yourself in this immediate area, or were you there at all times?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, corresponding to the needs of the service and the orders of the superior command, I was transferred from the Pirot garrison to Djakovica in 1997, in December 1997. It was a regular transfer to cater to the needs of the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you were the commander of the 2nd Motorised Company; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, I was commander of the 2nd Motorised Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Promoted to major when?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: I was promoted to major by regular procedure. I think the order was dated the 7th of May, 1998, and I was informed of it in October 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So within 1998 you were passing from being known as captain to being known as major; yes?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Yes, because my establishment position was captain first class, major, and after a certain number of years spent in that rank, the following rank was my entitlement. So I was promoted by regular procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How many men were in your company, please?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: My company numbered about 110 men, with the proviso that it was located in different places. It was practically never in one and the same location.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There was a rotation of troops into and out of a company like yours; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: No, there was no rotation. Those soldiers were admitted for their regular military service, and from training centres they were transferred to our unit. So there was no rotation of soldiers from other units or within our unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were soldiers in your unit introduced into the unit on the basis that they might be leaving after a year, then being retained, particularly because of the developing problems with the expected or possible NATO attack?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, those were soldiers who were serving their regular military service, and at that time it was 12 months. So on the basis of the situation in the country, which was immediate threat of war, their regular military service was extended by three months. And the same was done with the reserve force.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They could have been expecting to leave, say, in March of 1999, but they may be required to stay on a little longer; yes?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Included in the -- you might not remember all of a hundred names, of course. It might be difficult to do that. But we can probably identify some of the people who were in your company. One of them is Lieutenant Rade Radojevic, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, Rade Radojevic, Lieutenant, used to be a former commander of mine. In February I handed over my unit to another commander, whereas I received a motorised company. So he was a platoon commander. In February 1999, I took over another unit. Until that time, he was my commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Milan Markovic was a squad commander; is that right? Do you remember him?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: No. That name is not familiar to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He had no rank, but he was nevertheless at the time in command of a squad. Do you accept that that might be the position, that you have someone with no rank but nevertheless in charge of a squad?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, in our units that is not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Some other names that I can just jog your memory with. Do you remember the name Branko Kozarski?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Slobodan Gavrilovie, Slobodan -- probably Gavrilovje, I should think.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: In my unit, in the battalion where I worked, in the garrison in Djakovica, there was no such man. Maybe he worked in the brigade command in Prizren. But I had no contact with such a person.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nenad Milosavljevic?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: No. I don't know that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... wasn't in your company and that you can remember all the hundred or so names, or are you saying you don't remember the name?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I never said I remembered all the names. That's something you said. At the time, I knew everybody's name and I knew how much everybody was worth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The uniforms that you were wearing, you've spoken of an M88. Was there an M89?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: That could be a mistake. Those were camouflage, green uniforms; M89 or M93, they are the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did your unit have those uniforms?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Yes. Those were camouflage uniforms, of that type.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your unit used AP model 70 automatic rifles?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Yes. M70, 62 millimetres in calibre -- sorry; 7.62 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Shoulder patches with the two-headed eagle; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: No. We had patches only on our berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were gas masks occasionally provided and used?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: As far as I know, Mr. Nice, we never used gas masks. Only when there was a possibility of NATO air strike and when we suspected that they were using chemical projectiles would we put on gas masks. Because those were very peculiar explosions, producing a very peculiar particular cloud, and when we passed through such an area that had suffered from the impact of such an explosion, we would get orders to put on gas masks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you recall the assignment of any additional troops or particular individuals in March of 1999 to your company?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, the witness said: "And then I ordered my soldiers -- I would order my soldiers in such a case to put on gas masks," whereas the transcript says "then we would get orders to get masks."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: If the witness spoke at a normal rate of speech, this wouldn't happen. He's speaking on fast-forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you hear that? The interpreter is saying that you're still speaking too fast, and that is the explanation for some of the misinterpretations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, as for your question, some Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. soldiers came to my unit from training centres. I wouldn't get any other soldiers by transfer. They would come to me in batches as they arrived. We had no other source of reinforcement. After call-up, in April, the unit was reinforced to the level of wartime establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Travel to Djakovica for newly engaged soldiers from Pristina would be by bus, I think; yes?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there a particular officer, a captain, in your company charged with security duties?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Depending on the direction in which the soldiers went, they were accompanied by a physical security detail to prevent possible terrorist attacks against the column. I don't know what other security you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there a particular officer, a captain, charged with security duties, a man of quite strong personality - thinking back - in your company?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: No. In my company, I did not have a security organ. It was the battalion commander that had a security organ, and that duty was discharged by Lieutenant Nesovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Lieutenant --? So not a captain. Nesovic.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Yes. I think he was later promoted to captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is he a man of strong character, as you might recall?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: I don't know in which sense you mean it; physical or mental.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mental.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: He was responsible for security in our unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He was responsible for security in your unit. Thank you. And might he have been being called captain in the period 1998 or 1999?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I don't know. I think he was promoted by regular procedure to the rank of captain. But since I had little contact with him, because I didn't have that sort of problems in my unit, I don't know exactly when he was promoted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Your barracks were where in Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: My barracks in Djakovica was close to the Renik River at the exit from Djakovica town, facing Brekovac neighbourhood. Next to the barracks there was a Catholic church, or rather, a convent, a Catholic school.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is there a barracks in Djakovica known, or known colloquially, as the old barracks?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Yes. It is in the centre of the town. That's where this other unit was located, Djosan's unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were the police located in the old barracks?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: No. Police were not deployed in the old barracks. There was just one unit from that composition. The police had their own building at the exit from Djakovica town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There was one unit of the police in the old barracks; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: One unit occasionally spent time in our barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In your barracks. Very well. But this is not to be -- this is separate from the old barracks, is it?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: No. There was no such thing in the old barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there also the use of something that might be described as a field for location of some of your troops?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, before all those events started there, according to the regular plan of training of units, in April 1998 we went out to camp duty in the area of Sulane, above Babaj Baks, and that's where our unit went on encampment for regular training.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I'm grateful for that.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: That was in April 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It was. And at a later stage in the period with which we are concerned, 1998, your unit was deployed in the area of Radonjicko Jezero, the lake to the north of Djakovica, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Yes. One of my platoons there was securing roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you just look at this map, which I have to tell you was prepared on the basis not of any document provided by you as exhibits, we have marked, and we've already acknowledged the accuracy of this in general terms, places where your unit served. If we look at this map, we can see, in the bottom left-hand corner, circled, the areas which I'm going to suggest to you were areas where your units were camped and engaged. Sulane is one place which has already been referred to by you, as has Babaj Baks, Sisman Baks, and Sisman itself, and that was from April 1998; correct?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, it's true that the camp premises was in Sulane. There was no soldier in Babaj Baks. As for Suse Radni [phoen], those were terrorist strongholds. I don't know who made those circles here. There was not a single soldier of ours in either Sisman Radni [phoen] or Sisman Baks. Those were terrorist strongholds.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's look at the top part of the map, around the lake, Radonjicko lake. And we can see to the left, to the west, Gornji and Donji Bites, Rakoc, and then, is it just Don at the top, and then Raskoc or Rashkoc? Yes? These are all places in which you and your unit was engaged later on?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: No, Mr. Nice. The deployment of other units is something I have no clue about. According to superior command orders, I provided only one platoon for assistance up there. Radojevic was the commander of that platoon to secure the dam. I don't know about the deployment of other units. I don't know if any other units were present in that location.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were there any examples of any members of your company committing offences that had to be dealt with as criminal offences?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, there were no such incidents in my unit. I combated that sort of thing and I did not allow my soldiers to engage in any such thing. And if such a thing had happened, I immediately reported to the superior command, which contacted, in their turn, the authorities and the military police unit. If such a thing had happened, I would have done that. It didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the transcript says "If such a thing happened ..." or "If such a thing had happened ..." whereas the witness says, "If anybody had attempted such a thing, I would have immediately reported."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He didn't say it happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If, yes; conditional.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not even an attempt.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In all the time from April 1998 through to June 1999, the hundred men under your command, or more, not one of them fell for reporting for a criminal offence. Did any of them fall to be dealt with for a disciplinary offence?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, at that time, when I was in command of the unit, and in February, when I took over another unit, there was not a single case of either disciplinary proceedings against either a soldier or a commanding officer, for any attempt of illegal action or lack of discipline or any other sort of conduct that you are trying to allege.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Or even desertion? Desertion?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Desertion. Was anybody pursued at all or recorded as meriting pursuit on the ground of desertion?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: No, not that I know of. There were cases in June when a group of soldiers from the area of Sulane, a group of four soldiers, deserted the unit, and after that they provided all sorts of statements about alleged actions and that sort of thing. However, that unit was not engaged in any actions or any combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's break that down. Four soldiers. Can we have their names?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly. I know that they were from Montenegro, of Muslim faith.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you say that they made all sorts of statements about alleged actions and that sort of thing. First, when did they make these statements; and second, to whom?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, those soldiers came to my unit sometime in early June. We were in a camp, and on day two they left the unit, left the camp, and went nobody knew where. Later I found out the terrorists caught them and they gave statements to terrorists, who organised their transfer to Albania and later from Albania to Montenegro. So it is to them that they gave these statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... only been with you briefly, you obviously know the sort of statements and alleged actions and that sort of thing that they were referring to, so perhaps you'd tell us what they alleged.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Those allegations lead us to conclude that the soldiers had taken part in some combat operations, combat operations which never took place. So they were ready-made stories, ready-made statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Be so good as to answer the questions and we'll move along that much more quickly. "They provided all sorts of statements -" we've got the routing of the statements - "about alleged actions and that sort of thing." So what alleged action, what sort of thing were they making up in their statements? Tell us.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, they gave statements in the way that the terrorists had prepared them. That's the kind of statements they gave. Because those soldiers did not take part in any combat operations. They had only been in the unit for two days and they were being regularly trained in camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Please answer the question. You say the statements are made up. We can deal with that more and later. But what did they allege as against your group? Was it looting? Was it killing? Was it rape?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I'm not aware of any such statements. What I learnt from the information media, according to them, allegedly they had said they had taken part in some sort of combat operations, that they burnt houses. However, that's just not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we are about five minutes beyond the time for the break, so we'll adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you remembered the name of any of the four deserters?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I can't remember. It was a long time ago. It was June 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What we can be sure of is that it can't be those deserters, making the statements that they did, who provided the information on the map that we've just looked at, the information that's broadly accurate, identifying the two areas where you deployed, because those men were only present in your unit for a couple of days; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, my unit, when it took in that generation of soldiers, went to the Sulane camp area, so after the first day, those four soldiers deserted. There were never any combat operations that that generation of soldiers were engaged in, because they haven't even -- hadn't even completed their training.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before the date you give for the desertion of those four soldiers, in June of 1999, in May of 1999 there were two other men who deserted. Do you remember the two Koljevic cousins? I think it's Koljevic, but it may be Colovic.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: No, Mr. Nice. I think you've mixed things up. You say 1999. What I'm saying was in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I'm concerned with then two men who deserted much later. In May of 1999, two men of Muslim ethnicity were still in your company, they were cousins. Their names were Colovic, and they deserted. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I never had two such soldiers in my unit. The only four soldiers in June 1998 who left the unit of their own accord and took off in an unknown direction, but there were no other instances of that, apart from those four soldiers, and this is the first time that I hear of these two soldiers that you're mentioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: These two soldiers went to Macedonia and then to Bosnia, where they were spoken to by investigators of this Tribunal. Their initial explanations were recorded. They were invited to repeat them on tape, but for fear of one kind or another, they declined to put them on tape. But their original allegations exist, and I'm going to put those allegations to you. Think back. The man Ersad Colovic asserts that he explained to investigators that he was due to be rotated out after his year of service on the 18th of March of 1999, but that was cancelled, first of all for one month and then totally. And you remember answering my questions about people who might have been rotated out. Does my account -- or does the account that Esad Colovic gave make sense?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, that's not correct, and there's no sense to it. All soldiers, pursuant to orders by the supreme command, had their military service extended by three months, because when faced with the danger of war and the start of the NATO aggression against our country, those soldiers could not have been dismissed from the army because the units would have been left empty. We wouldn't have had any soldiers to carry out our operations with, and I hear about this soldier for the first time now. So it's impossible that -- it is impossible that his military service was extended for one month and then was rotated out. So despite the fact that a three-month period was given, these soldiers went back to the same unit, or rather, stayed in the same unit. And there was no rotation at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm happy to put these investigators' notes on the overhead projector. Of course, I'm not expecting them to be admitted as exhibits. If I put them on the overhead projector, then of course they can be made available to the accused. Otherwise, I'll put them simply as allegations, but it would probably be easier if we could put them on the overhead projector so that we can see them, because of course they're not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, let them be put --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At page -- in which case we'll go through them quickly. At page 5, please. These are not in English, Mr. Sel. If you don't read English, I'm afraid you'll have to make do with the interpretation. The passage I've just read out is a little bit further down that page, please, Mr. Prendergast. "Was due to be rotated out at the conclusion of his year service." We must go -- he deals with the 1st Motorised Platoon and Radojevic on that page. Can we go to the next page, please. What's said -- next page, please, Mr. Prendergast. Thank you. The bottom of the page, Joint Operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What is said against -- not against. What is said about conduct of affairs generally, and this starts in 1998, is that there were joint operations with the police. Is it right that there were, in 1998 and 1999, joint operations with the police?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we performed our assignments pursuant to orders from our superior command. There were no joint operations. They did their job, we did ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who did the clearing up of the battlefield, then?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: I don't know in what sense, clearing up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll have to move forward a little bit, but I'll come back to this document in a second. In the operation of the 24th to the 30th of March, the VJ lost three soldiers, and how many KLA were killed?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, as far as I know, my unit had just one casualty, one soldier killed when the tank turned over just in front of the village of Mamusa. I had no other casualties. I don't know what the situation was like, of course, in other units. But what I said was that, as far as the terrorists are concerned -- as far as the terrorists are concerned, Mr. Nice, they had a very well elaborated system for pulling out their dead and wounded, co-fighters, so that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've explained this before and it has to be brief. You're actually saying, are you, that in a time when the full force of the VJ surrounds the KLA, they not only fire on the VJ from time to time, but when they suffer casualties, they manage to physically remove the bodies; is that what you're saying, and that's their priority? Nonsense, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, it's not nonsense. The object of it was to get the dead and wounded terrorists away from the area because there were quite a lot of mercenaries amongst their ranks. Foreign mercenaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Foreign mercenaries. They had to get the dead away because, what, this would implicate some foreign country, or why? Why is that so important? A mercenary is a mercenary. He gets paid to run the risk of dying. Why would they have to be moved?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I don't know about that. You'd have to ask them that. So bring them in and ask them. I don't know why they were pulled out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, this page, the top deals with the accommodation at the old barracks in Djakovica. It was suggested that the police didn't -- with whom you worked - you're denying that there were any joint operations - did not appear to be regular MUP, and indeed took pills. Do you remember any incident of the MUP that you had contact with taking pills for reasons?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, what you've just been saying are just ad hoc facts that you are trying to place. They were regular police units, carrying out their assignments. Some of them were in their -- our building because there wasn't enough space in their own SUP building, because that's where the offices were and their accommodation was in our barracks. So they used our barracks just for accommodation, that is, to spend the night. And the pills, who took what pills, I really don't know. I can't say. I don't know where you get that from. We don't need pills.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, bottom of the page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The condition of the monitor is not good. It's difficult to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The contrast should be adjusted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, the source of this information says, as against you and the way you operated things, that his platoon worked with two others, and there was a systematic method of working with a mortar platoon, a hand-held rocket platoon who would conduct initial bombardments of villages being attacked, and then his platoon would be responsible for the actual cleansing. Now, first of all, did your units work in coordinated groups of three platoons, in the way he suggests?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I assume that the witness isn't receiving any interpretation, because since Mr. Nice started I haven't heard a single word of the interpretation. I'm not sure if the witness is receiving any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me ask him. Have you been receiving interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Nice, let's -- could you ask the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you hear me now, Mr. Sel? Is it right that your troops worked in coordinated deployments of three platoons?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean. My company had three rifle platoons, so I don't know which deployments you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there a mortar platoon?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Yes, there was a rifle support unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there a hand-held rocket platoon?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Yes. That is based on establishment in a rifle platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what is being suggested by this person to the investigators was that cleansing of villages was done in a coordinated way, with the mortar platoon and the hand-held rocket platoon bombarding the village first, and the other, the third platoon, going in and cleansing the village. Is that what happened? 1998 and 1999.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, that is just not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And if we look at the next passage, he goes on to explain --

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Allow me to explain. Hand-held rocket launchers that the soldiers had have a range of 200 metres. You have to come up close to the fortified place, up to 150 metres away from it, to be able to target it. Second, we didn't use any mortars in those operations. I said that a moment ago in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... have been destroyed, haven't they? All your records, including the records of the ammunition you've used, they've all been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, in the daily combat reports to the superior command that the units sent up to the brigade, you could see how much ammunition we used and how much ammunition we needed to replenish our supplies. So if you apply the term "shelling," if you're going to apply the term "shelling," within my composition I had 120 mines for mortars. What can you destroy with those 120 mines? You can't destroy an inhabited or built-up area of 25 houses. That's just an illusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... read on because we're very pressed for time. He explained that your method of conduct of operations was this: That before leaving camp, they wouldn't be briefed, the soldiers, as to what they were doing. They would be told they were going to be attacking a KLA stronghold. But that in reality, in the period of time he was there, no KLA strongholds were found.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, KLA strongholds -- you're mixing that up with terrorist strongholds. There was no KLA, Kosovo Liberation Army, down there. What was there were terrorists, and we destroyed the terrorist strongholds. I explained that to you a moment ago, with the materiel evidence we found, the list of terrorists, the number of weapons, the plans of defence. And all the soldiers, before going out on assignment, were informed in detail with the security measures, with the international war law and conduct vis-a-vis prisoners of war, and so on and so forth. So they always knew which assignment they were going on and where. And otherwise, I was at the head of those soldiers, so I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Exactly. And he makes it plain -- shall we turn over the page, please, Mr. Prendergast -- that it was you, in nearly all occasions, who was the person who gave instructions to kill civilians. I'll just explain to you what he says, and I'm going to read from the paragraph just above where we are, Mr. Prendergast. "The infantry would approach the village and get to the tall walls that surround the yards -" that's the yards of Kosovo Albanians' houses - "throw tear gas over the wall and enter wearing gas masks. Entry would be made into both yards and houses. The witness states they would be looking for wounded persons or persons that needed assistance. [And] states that depending on the mood of the Company Commander sometimes they would get the order to kill people or certain people other times no one would be killed." He's basically saying that the decision to kill was made at the site and it was made by you. Is he right in that?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, first of all, I don't know who that soldier is at all. I'd like you to bring him in here so that we can -- I could confront him, tete-a-tete, and to see before the Judges what is true and what is not. What you have just read is just not right. It's -- the question is who he made the statement to. I'd like to know that. Because I never issued any such orders to my soldiers. First of all, I didn't train them to kill innocent civilians or to burn and destroy and do things that they weren't supposed to do. Soldiers were trained, we all know for what purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, he goes on to explain in more detail how, when they first arrived, you told them they were not to kill civilians, only the KLA. He says that during the first days of his deployment, there was only one ambush. They were expecting the KLA from Albania, but no one came. Is it right that there was a time when you did give express orders that civilians were not to be killed?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, when any assignment was to be carried out, all the soldiers received strict orders as to what assignments or orders they should execute and what not. Anything outside the orders issued would go against the grain of regulations and be opposed to regulations. So they never received orders to destroy civilians or cultural monuments or set fire to houses or anything like that. Now, as far as the ambush is concerned, yes, the unit was engaged in keeping the frontier secure in depth, with patrols and ambushes, which was the only way we could stop the infiltration of weapons from Albania into the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. But we never opened fire first.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The source of this information is clearly right in the next paragraph. He says you appeared to be friendly, appeared to be pleasant. "We had the same --" later on it wasn't the same, is the way the investigators recorded it, he said: "We had the same company commander the entire time. He did get promoted from captain first class to major. The major never issued orders directly to a single soldier. He would issue them to the whole squad. That way, everyone would shoot." Now, you've heard the suggestion from this source, and I'm going to suggest to you that this is exactly how killing and ethnic cleansing occurs, because, as you will know from your experience, it's people at your level who were given the power over life and death, knowing that you'd never be sanctioned for killing civilians. Is that what happened, that you gave instructions to your platoons to kill everyone?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, first of all, what you've just said is just not true. Those are arbitrary conclusions on your part. And I never was in command of a squad. I was in command of a company. So the conclusions you draw are just not right. My soldiers were never given orders to kill innocent civilians or to fire on features that were not used to fire at us. And you are referring to some witness statements that I have never heard of.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, the same source suggests that you also had women brought to your troops, and that this was one of your preferred activities. Just tell us: Were there occasions of women coming to your troops at camps and elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, that is absolute nonsense, quite incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is it?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: That never happened, nor did I do anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Didn't you? Because before we come to that --

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- one matter of detail. Remember I asked you about the security officer who you said was promoted to captain, a person of strong personality? Do you remember an incident at a lake, when you were so cross with a soldier who had gone in the lake that you put a gun to his head and were deterred from going further by a security officer, captain? Do you remember that incident?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, first of all, I was never at that lake. There was just one platoon sent to that lake, Radonjicko lake. And second, I never carried a rifle; I carried an automatic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's not clear from the notes whether it's that particular lake, it's only described here as "a lake." But where the detail given by this source is of a captain, a security officer, who had the courage to confront his commanding officer, that fits with the description of the captain you confirmed to me, doesn't it? Lieutenant, later Captain, Nesovic?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: I never had that kind of confrontation with my superior or, for that matter, with my subordinate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Bottom of the page, please. You know, don't you, that -- well, for all women, reporting rape is a difficult business. For Kosovo Albanian women, it is almost impossible because of the consequences for the rest of their lives of being someone who has been raped. You know that. It's a cultural fact. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I don't know what you're getting at. But let me repeat: There were no women in my area of defence that were brought in or taken away or anything like that. Those are arbitrary statements. Let me repeat again: I don't know where you got those statements from or who gave them to you, because it's just not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next page, please. He says that a large number of women, 35 or 36 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be provided with a copy of the indictment that Mr. Nice is quoting from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice, please let the accused have a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is it in B/C/S, which might assist the witness? Because we're looking at a document that's been written in English by someone and the witness doesn't apparently know that person. But if it was in the original state, the witness could check content of the material.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's been written by investigators, in English.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Written by investigators, in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we look at this page, the suggestion is a large number of women, 35 or 36, were brought to Sulane. You were at Sulane, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, the system of organisation in the army implies that where the army is stationed, there is no access to civilians, women, or anybody else. Even my own mother wouldn't be able to enter camp. Now, what you've been saying, that never happened. Things like that never happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Go to -- let's go to the bottom of this page, please. He identifies -- I've read the names out. I'm not going to reread them. You can see them on the screen. Kozarski and three others, included in the soldiers who raped women. Thinking back, is there some truth in this or is it all entirely made up, do you say?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, this has been made up entirely. None of my soldiers left the area of defence at all. That was strictly forbidden. So any attempt at doing so, at leaving the area, would entail reporting to the military police and steps taken afterwards to sanction the perpetrator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is there any point to all this? This isn't even a witness statement. And just like everything else that Mr. Nice is trying to launch, it's all science fiction. I don't know how anyone can take it seriously.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Milosevic's microphone be adjusted, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
